newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin to have heart surgery - spokesman.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to have heart surgery - spokesman.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin has agreed to have a heart operation, probably at the end of the month in Moscow, the head of his press service said on Thursday.
He said the 65-year-old Kremlin leader had made the announcement in an interview filmed on Thursday by the Russian RIA news agency's television unit.

Interfax news agency quoted journalists present at the filming of the interview as saying Yeltsin explained that doctors who established he had heart problems had given him a choice -- undergoing an operation or "working passively".
"B. Yeltsin said that passive work has 'never suited him'. That is why he has decided to recover in full through an operation," Interfax said.
Yeltsin, evidently alluding to earlier speculation he would have surgery abroad, said he was going to have his operation in Russia.

"Our cardiological centre is capable of conducting such operations. I think it is fitting for the president to have an operation at home, in the motherland," he said, adding he hoped for support from the nation.
The interview would be shown at 6 or 7 p.m. (1400 or 1500 GMT), Ignatyev said.
The spokesman did not specify what kind of heart operation Yeltsin would have.
Yeltsin, who had two heart attacks last year, disappeared from public view shortly before winning a second term in office on July 3.
Aides had so far denied that he was ill, saying only that the president was exhausted after a gruelling election campaign.

Yeltsin's chief of staff, Anatoly Chubais, said on Wednesday that the rumours of ill health had ben caused by an inadequate information policy on the part of the Kremlin and pledged to make serious changes.
RIA said Yeltsin also spoke in the interview about U.S. air raids on Iraq and the latest peace deal with Chechen rebels.

He said he intended to raise the issue of the U.S. air raids during his meeting with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, which is scheduled for Saturday at Yeltsin's country residence, where he has been taking a holiday.
The presidential press service said earlier on Thursday that Yeltsin backed his government in denouncing the raids.
Yeltsin also spoke about the peace deal which his security chief Alexander Lebed signed with Chechen separatists last week. The president has not expressed an opinion on the deal publicly.

His last televised interview, a brief five-minute affair also with the previously little known RIA television, was exactly two weeks ago, when he criticised Lebed's progress in peace negotiations. On that occasion and on subsequent brief clips on television news, Yeltsin looked stiff but relatively relaxed.
